Robert Pollard.summary: Dayton, OH songwriter whose first billed solo album extended Guided by Voices' four-track jump-cut hooks into an even more fragmented, private home-taped world.

Rodney Crowell.summary: Nashville songwriter whose Telecaster-driven, guest-heavy roots records set a plainspoken pattern that carried him from cult favorite to chart-topping country hitmaker.
Rodney Crowell.related: Emmylou Harris; Guy Clark; Rosanne Cash

Rolling Blackouts Coastal Fever.summary: Melbourne trio whose three interlocking guitars and plainspoken, road-trip lyrics make them one of the cleanest modern distillations of Flying Nun/Go-Betweens jangle-pop.

Rosali.summary: Philadelphia-rooted songwriter whose plainspoken, patient folk unravels slowly, opening into fuller guitar-forward rock through her ongoing partnership with a Nebraska backing band.

Rosanne Cash.summary: Nashville singer whose rock-informed, gloss-averse country records moved from chart-topping honky-tonk hits to a stark, self-produced turn toward confessional songwriting.
Rosanne Cash.related: Rodney Crowell; Guy Clark; Emmylou Harris

Rose City Band.summary: Ripley Johnson's Portland solo project trades his psych-rock band's krautrock drone for warm, pedal-steel-laced homage to 1970s cosmic country rock.

Rosie Flores.summary: LA cowpunk veteran who went solo for a straighter rockabilly-and-honky-tonk major-label debut that briefly crossed her into mainstream country radio.

Royal Trux.summary: New York noise-rock duo whose extreme, uncompromising early Drag City records helped establish the label's tolerance for difficult, DIY-damaged music.

Rubber Rodeo.summary: Rhode Island art-school band crossing new-wave synths and drum machines with pedal steel and close vocal harmony, an East Coast cousin to LA's cowpunk scene.

Ruby of Thanks.summary: Drummer for several bands who records intimate, handmade home songs under this name, sitting in the Woodsist-orbit lo-fi home-taping tradition.

Rui Gabriel.summary: Solo debut from a member of a sing-along power-pop and post-punk band, using a lighter palette of fun grooves to write self-aware songs about class and miscommunication.

Russ Tolman.summary: True West co-founder whose solo debut traded that band's guitar noise for cleaner, narrative country-rock songwriting about Western landscapes and small lives.

Ruston Kelly.summary: Nashville songwriter who coined his own "dirt emo" tag, bending outlaw and neo-traditional country vocabulary toward emo's confessional, diary-like mode.

Rusty Wier.summary: Austin dancehall fixture whose best-known record delivers hard-strummed, good-time honky-tonk rock built for the rowdier bar-band side of the 1970s scene.

Ryan Adams.summary: Whiskeytown alumnus whose prolific solo catalog ran from spare acoustic breakup records through classic rock, honky-tonk and jam-band detours across a Lost Highway decade.

Ryan Davis & the Roadhouse Band.summary: Louisville songwriter fronting a barfly-rock band whose wordy, tragicomic double-LP songwriting extends the Silver Jews/David Berman lineage into the 2020s.
Ryan Davis & the Roadhouse Band.related: State Champion; David Berman; Silver Jews

Ryley Walker.summary: Chicago fingerpicker who fused folk songwriting with jazz improvisation into loose, Van Morrison-and-Tim-Buckley-indebted jams before pushing into harder-edged studio experimentation.

S.G. Goodman.summary: Western-Kentucky songwriter whose rocking, rootsy debut and darker, fuzzier follow-up made her a leading voice of the post-Tyler Childers Kentucky scene.

Sadurn.summary: Philadelphia songwriter whose spare, diary-like full-band debut folk is indebted to Jason Molina, Gillian Welch and Elliott Smith.

Saintseneca.summary: Zac Little's Columbus, OH string-band project blending dulcimer, mandolin and balalaika Appalachian instrumentation with denser, electric indie folk-rock across two decades.

Salem 66.summary: Boston Homestead-label band pairing twin vocal harmonies over ringing, mid-tempo guitar rock, gentler and more melodic than noisier labelmates.

Sam Amidon.summary: Vermont songwriter reworking old-time and traditional ballads into spare, occasionally jazz-inflected arrangements descended from the Anthology of American Folk Music tradition.

Sam Blasucci.summary: Mapache member's solo detour trading intertwined acoustic guitars for a piano-led, fully autobiographical songwriting voice about settling into adult life.

Sam Burton.summary: Los Angeles (via Salt Lake City) singer whose high, Roy Orbison-like wail rides moody, echo-laden country-rock production.

Sam Evian.summary: Sam Owens's warm, lightly psychedelic bedroom-folk project that grew into the Catskills recording hub he built and produces from as Flying Cloud Studios.

Sam Moss.summary: Virginia-based (New England-born) fingerstyle guitarist whose raspy, earthy folk draws on the same Appalachian/American Primitive lineage as other song-collecting pickers.
Sam Moss.related: Califone; Megafaun; Mountain Goats; Mountain Man

Sam Outlaw.summary: Los Angeles songwriter working the smooth, string-laced Southern California countrypolitan tradition rather than rowdier outlaw twang.

Sammi Smith.summary: Outlaw-era Nashville singer whose smoky hit reading of a then-unknown Kris Kristofferson song made her one of the movement's few prominent female voices.

Sandy Bull.summary: New York guitarist whose raga- and jazz-inflected banjo-and-electric-guitar debut predates and runs parallel to the Takoma American Primitive scene.
Sandy Bull.related: Robbie Basho; Marisa Anderson; Chuck Johnson

Sandy Denny.summary: British folk-rock singer whose Fairport/Fotheringay-rooted solo albums moved from electric folk-rock toward increasingly orchestrated, then cabaret-tinged songwriting.

Sarah Shook & the Disarmers.summary: Chapel Hill band whose raw, high-lonesome blend of honky-tonk twang and punk attitude built a defiant, road-worn reputation across a Bloodshot-era decade.
Sarah Shook & the Disarmers.related: Sarah Shook and the Devil; Sarah Shook and the Dirty Hands

Say Sue Me.summary: Busan, South Korea band whose warm, reverb-drenched jangle-pop transplants Flying Nun/Byrds tones into a consistently pristine throwback indie-rock run.

Scott H. Biram.summary: Austin one-man-band whose distorted solo mix of blues, punk and honky-tonk applies Bloodshot's insurgent-country ethos to raw, punk-blues extremity.

Scout Niblett.summary: English songwriter whose stark, deadpan-to-shouted guitar-or-piano-and-drums records joined Drag City's roster of raw, minimalist confessional artists.

Scrawl.summary: Columbus, Ohio band led by Marcy Mays and Sue Harshe playing rough, unglamorous Midwestern guitar rock out of the Homestead/Rough Trade college-rock network.

Screamin' Sirens.summary: All-female Hollywood cowpunk band mixing country, rockabilly and punk with a rowdy, gang-like energy on the LA club circuit of the early 1980s.

Screaming Trees.summary: Eastern-Washington band pairing Mark Lanegan's deep baritone with psychedelic, Crazy Horse-adjacent guitar work, a critical favorite within the Seattle grunge scene.

Scud Mountain Boys.summary: Joe Pernice's Northampton band whose quiet, pedal-steel-laced country-rock, played at near-lullaby tempo, bridged 1990s alt-country storytelling and slowcore's hushed sadness.

Sea Level.summary: Allman Brothers spinoff formed by three of that band's members for a jazzier, fusion-leaning take on the Capricorn Southern-rock sound.

Seam.summary: Sooyoung Park's post-Bitch Magnet Chicago band whose patient, hushed-to-loud dynamics helped define 1990s slowcore and influence the emo scenes that followed.

Sean Thompson's Weird Ears.summary: Nashville sideman's solo project moving from a modest EP to a fuller, cosmic-country-jam debut LP after years of touring for other artists.

Sebadoh.summary: Lou Barlow's post-Dinosaur Jr. band whose raw four-track home-tape collages, split between his confessionals and Eric Gaffney's noise, became a defining lo-fi touchstone.

Shabason & Krgovich.summary: Joseph Shabason and Nicholas Krgovich's chamber-pop duo reaching for CD-era country-rock glow inspired by Neil Young and k.d. lang.

Shallowater.summary: Houston band (with West Texas roots) whose self-described "raw West Texas dirtgaze" swallows dusty country guitar figures in walls of overdriven shoegaze noise.

Shania Twain.summary: Nashville-produced pop-country crossover whose Mutt Lange-produced arena-pop records became the best-selling country album by a woman ever.

Shannon Lay.summary: Los Angeles songwriter whose spare, Nick Drake/Vashti Bunyan-indebted folk grew fuller after she left a punk band for a dedicated solo career.

Sharon Van Etten.summary: Brooklyn songwriter whose stark, confessional debut grew into a fuller indie-rock sound once the National's Aaron Dessner began producing her.

Sharp Pins.summary: Kai Slater's Chicago solo power-pop project delivering bedroom-recorded, Big Star/Teenage Fanclub-style hooks released through Calvin Johnson's own imprint.

She Returns From War.summary: Hunter Park's South Carolina project billing itself "Cosmic Americana," blending country roots with dance-pop production and wry Nashville needling.

Shearwater.summary: Jonathan Meiburg's project that began as an Okkervil River side band before growing into its own delicate, dynamically extreme chamber-folk act.

Sheepskin.summary: Burlington, Vermont duo making tasteful, close-harmony dual-vocal folk in the old Canvasback/Asthmatic Kitty vein.

Shel Silverstein.summary: Cartoonist and children's author who was also a prolific Nashville country songwriter, collecting his own comic story-songs including a hit later popularized by Johnny Cash.
Shel Silverstein.related: Johnny Cash; Bobby Bare; Dr. Hook & the Medicine Show

Shep Treasure.summary: Rochester songwriter making hazy, meditative folk rock that pairs gorgeousness with eeriness and murky, slowcore-adjacent production.

Shirley Collins and Davy Graham.summary: A landmark collaboration setting traditional English and American folk songs against Davy Graham's blues- and jazz-inflected fingerstyle guitar, foundational to British folk-rock.
Shirley Collins and Davy Graham.related: Bert Jansch; John Renbourn; John Martyn; Fairport Convention

Shoes.summary: Zion, Illinois band whose four-track home-recorded debut built genuine Beatles/Big Star melodicism almost entirely from guitars and harmony, an early bedroom-pop blueprint.

Shoulderbird.summary: Chicago songwriter's modest, home-recorded project of intimate Midwest Americana about moving, displacement and family.

Shrunken Elvis.summary: Instrumental Nashville sideman trio exploring kosmische, ambient and jazz-fusion textures born from a European tour's worth of jamming.
Shrunken Elvis.related: Spencer Cullum's Coin Collection; Sean Thompson's Weird Ears

Sierra Ferrell.summary: West Virginia-to-Nashville songwriter blending bluegrass and old-time instrumentation with vintage country, gypsy-jazz and folk textures into a genuinely idiosyncratic voice.

Silkworm.summary: Missoula-to-Seattle-to-Chicago band led by two songwriters whose lean, riff-driven, literate guitar rock moved through Matador and Touch and Go across a decade-plus run.

Silver Jews.summary: David Berman's Drag City band, formed with Pavement's Stephen Malkmus and Bob Nastanovich, whose deadpan, aphoristic songwriting became the touchstone for wry indie-country storytelling.
Silver Jews.related: Pavement; Stephen Malkmus; Bob Nastanovich; MJ Lenderman

Silver Synthetic.summary: New Orleans garage-punk veteran's pivot toward warm, chiming '70s classic rock and cosmic pop.

Sima Cunningham.summary: Chicago songwriter (one half of a DIY-scene duo) whose ornate, emotionally heavy solo debut moves from spare piano balladry to cathartic full arrangements.

Simon Joyner.summary: Omaha songwriter working independently but in strikingly similar deadpan, plainspoken narrative territory to early Silver Jews, later cited by Conor Oberst as a foundational influence.

Sinai Vessel.summary: Caleb Cordes's Asheville project that moved from twinkly emo toward heavier, patient, Americana-inflected indie rock about guilt, grief and the toll of touring.

Sir Douglas Quintet.summary: Doug Sahm's Texas band whose garage rock, Tex-Mex and homesick country hybrid made him a connective figure across the whole Texas music scene.
Sir Douglas Quintet.related: Bob Dylan; Willie Nelson; Flaco Jimenez

Skyway Man.summary: James Wallace's kaleidoscopic Oakland psych project mixing piano-led rock with dense arrangements and a wide cast of Nashville/Asheville cosmic-country guests.
Skyway Man.related: The Dead Tongues; Erin Rae; Vetiver; Spencer Cullum

Slaid Cleaves.summary: Austin-based, Maine-raised songwriter whose plainspoken, working-class character studies extend the Guy Clark/Townes Van Zandt Texas storytelling lineage into the 2000s.

Slaughter Beach, Dog.summary: Jake Ewald's post-Modern Baseball project moving from pop-punk urgency into loose, talky Americana and alt-country storytelling about small-town life.

Sleeper's Bell.summary: Chicago DIY-folk act making quiet, unhurried guitar-and-voice recordings with occasional full-band lift, released on a small spring vinyl pressing.

Sloan.summary: Halifax band that abandoned its grunge debut for a warmer, four-songwriter Beatles/Byrds/Kinks-style melody blend that became hugely influential on Canadian indie rock.

Slobberbone.summary: Denton, Texas band fronted by Brent Best playing loud, scrappy punk-and-country songwriting about small-town boredom and hard luck.

Slow Pulp.summary: Madison/Chicago band blending blown-out shoegaze guitar with increasingly hooky, Americana-tinged pop songwriting.

Slowdive.summary: Reading, UK shoegaze band that slowed My Bloody Valentine's roar into ambient-leaning dream pop, becoming the most cited touchstone for 2010s shoegaze revival bands.

Sluice.summary: Justin Morris's Durham, North Carolina project turning river-and-faith reflections into open-hearted, pastoral fingerpicked folk-rock.

Small Factory.summary: Providence duo making spare, deadpan boy-girl indie pop in the vein of early Beat Happening and Unrest.

Smog.summary: Bill Callahan's long-running Drag City project, moving from close-mic'd four-track confessionals through fuller, country-inflected arrangements before he began recording under his own name.

Snail Mail.summary: Lindsey Jordan's Baltimore project whose plainspoken, diaristic teenage debut of clean, jangly guitar-pop became a defining record of the 2010s slacker-rock revival.

Snapper.summary: Dunedin band built around founding Clean member Peter Gutteridge's droning, Velvet Underground-indebted guitar, pushing the scene's jangle toward heavier feedback-caked noise-rock.

Sneaky Feelings.summary: Dunedin band from the original Dunedin Double EP whose clean, 1960s-pop-indebted songwriting made them Flying Nun's most straightforwardly tuneful act.

Snocaps.summary: Surprise one-off project pairing the Crutchfield sisters with MJ Lenderman and Brad Cook for warm, harmony-driven indie rock, the sisters' first record together since their teenage punk band.

Soccer Mommy.summary: Sophie Allison's Nashville project that moved her Bandcamp bedroom-pop into full-band, 90s-alt-rock-indebted confessional songwriting about jealousy and self-doubt.

Social Distortion.summary: Orange County punk band whose pullback from hardcore speed into slower, twangier, Johnny Cash-inflected songwriting marked cowpunk's late entry point.

Son Volt.summary: Jay Farrar's post-Uncle Tupelo band whose somber, pedal-steel-heavy records became the definitive sound most people mean by 1990s insurgent country.

Songs: Ohia.summary: Jason Molina's stark, haunted Chicago project, moving from spare voice-and-guitar records to the Crazy Horse-scaled sound that led to his later band's name.
Songs: Ohia.related: Will Oldham; Palace; Alasdair Roberts; Magnolia Electric Co.

Sonic Youth.summary: New York band whose alternate-tuned, prepared-guitar no-wave noise evolved into structured, anthemic noise-rock across a run from SST to Geffen.

Soul Asylum.summary: Minneapolis Twin/Tone band whose melodic punk, produced early on by Husker Du's Bob Mould, carried a rootsier heartland-rock lean toward a mainstream crossover.

Souled American.summary: Chicago band whose glacially slow, dub-inflected pedal-steel country records became an unheralded root of alt-country's stranger, slower fringe.

Soundgarden.summary: Seattle band whose Sabbath/Zeppelin-indebted metal-leaning grunge helped push the genre onto hard-rock radio.

South San Gabriel.summary: Will Johnson's hushed, slow-tempo alter ego to his main band, exploring the slowcore-adjacent side of the Denton, Texas scene.

Souther-Hillman-Furay Band.summary: Country-rock supergroup pairing Byrds/Burritos bassist Chris Hillman and Poco founder Richie Furay with Laurel Canyon songwriter J.D. Souther.
Souther-Hillman-Furay Band.related: The Byrds; The Flying Burrito Brothers; Poco; J.D. Souther

Southern Culture on the Skids.summary: Chapel Hill band pairing surf-guitar twang with gleeful, self-aware trailer-park kitsch and B-movie Southern theater.

Spain.summary: Josh Haden's (son of bassist Charlie Haden) Los Angeles project setting a low, unhurried voice over minimal, jazz-inflected slowcore arrangements.

Sparklehorse.summary: Mark Linkous's Richmond, Virginia project built from hushed, hiss-laden home recordings that swing between fragile acoustic passages and sudden bursts of distortion.

Speedy Ortiz.summary: Sadie Dupuis's Northampton/Philadelphia band whose knotty, Guided-by-Voices/Pavement-indebted guitar riffs and sardonic lyrics defined a key 2010s slacker-noise-rock crossover.

Spencer Cullum's Coin Collection.summary: Nashville pedal-steel sideman Spencer Cullum's bandleader project turning his session work into English-folk-rock-inflected songwriting across a trilogy of albums.
Spencer Cullum's Coin Collection.related: Erin Rae; Andrew Combs; Rich Ruth

Spencer Hoffman.summary: Los Angeles songwriter making buoyant, bittersweet '70s-influenced folk-rock built on acoustic guitars, piano and orchestral touches.

Spencer Radcliffe.summary: Long-running solo songwriter (Chicago, then Ohio) whose early sparse home recordings eventually fed into fuzzy, hypnotic Midwest indie-twang.

Spoon.summary: Austin band that moved from noisy Pixies/Wire-indebted post-punk through a bruising major-label detour to the minimalist, rhythm-forward sound that defined their Merge Records run.

Squirrel Bait.summary: Teenage Louisville hardcore-turned-post-hardcore band whose members immediately scattered into two pillars of the American underground after this short-lived group split.

Squirrel Flower.summary: Ella Williams's evolving Chicago/Iowa project moving from hushed indie folk-rock toward dense, countrygaze-adjacent guitar-wall rock produced within the Asheville scene network.

Star Moles.summary: Prolific Bandcamp DIY songwriter making lo-fi home recordings with a loose, sci-fi-inflected sense of humor across ten-plus full-lengths.

State Champion.summary: Ryan Davis's main band before his solo Roadhouse Band project, playing loose, twangy "Beard Rock" built to carry his dense, surrealist wordplay.
State Champion.related: Ryan Davis & the Roadhouse Band; Catherine Irwin; Freakwater; David Berman

Steeleye Span.summary: Ashley Hutchings's (ex-Fairport Convention) harder-line electric folk band pushing British traditional song even further from rock-band conventions.

Stella Donnelly.summary: Perth songwriter whose plainspoken, funny-sad lyrics and light, jangly indie-folk arrangements grew out of the city's DIY scene.

Stephen Malkmus.summary: Pavement frontman's solo project, backed by the Jicks, extending that band's off-kilter guitar melodies and cryptic wordplay into looser, more classic-rock-leaning territory.

Steve Earle.summary: Nashville songwriter whose hard-Telecaster country-rock debut gave way, after prison, to a prolific, genre-hopping run of Americana and protest records that shaped the alt-country era.
Steve Earle.related: Guy Clark; The Del McCoury Band; The Pogues

Steve Earle & the Del McCoury Band.summary: Steve Earle's full album of original bluegrass, written for and performed live with a celebrated bluegrass band.
Steve Earle & the Del McCoury Band.related: The Del McCoury Band; Steve Earle

Steve Fromholz.summary: Austin-scene songwriter (later Texas poet laureate) whose wry, plainspoken character songs and much-covered "Texas Trilogy" made him a beloved fixture of the progressive-country movement.

Steve Goodman.summary: Chicago folk songwriter whose train travelogue song and tight partnership with John Prine anchored the city's mutually supportive early-1970s folk-club circuit.
Steve Goodman.related: John Prine; Bob Dylan; Jimmy Buffett

Steve Gunn.summary: Brooklyn/Philadelphia guitarist whose raga-inflected instrumental records grew into full-band, sun-warmed cosmic-country songwriting on Matador.

Steve Wynn.summary: Dream Syndicate frontman whose first solo album after that band's breakup traded noise-guitar sprawl for cleaner, song-focused Americana-facing roots rock.

Steve Young.summary: Nashville songwriter whose "Seven Bridges Road" (later an Eagles hit) and rough, plainspoken country-rock made him a direct forerunner of the outlaw movement.

Straitjacket Fits.summary: Dunedin band formed from ex-Verlaines and Bats members, pushing the scene's jangle toward louder, more distorted noise-pop.

Strand of Oaks.summary: Timothy Showalter's Philadelphia project moving from hushed, gothic folk records to arena-scaled, cathartic rock aided by My Morning Jacket and J Mascis.

Strange Ranger.summary: Missoula/Portland/Philadelphia band (formerly billed under another name) whose emo-tinged, twangy indie rock cycled through noisier and electronic phases before returning to guitars.

Sturgill Simpson.summary: Nashville songwriter whose straight hard-country debut gave way to psychedelic, genre-hopping "new outlaw" records spanning soul, arena rock and bluegrass.

Styrofoam Winos.summary: Three Nashville solo songwriters trading instruments and lead vocals for a shaggy-dog, Feelies-ish "patio album" sound tied to the city's dive-bar scene.
Styrofoam Winos.related: Ryan Davis & the Roadhouse Band; MJ Lenderman

Sufjan Stevens.summary: New York songwriter whose sprawling concept album pushed chamber-folk into theatrical baroque-pop before a later record stripped back to hushed, devastating acoustic songwriting.

Summer Dean.summary: Fort Worth songwriter whose confident, big-voiced honky-tonk about aging and ambition is a sturdy entry in the current Texas revival.
Summer Dean.related: Joshua Ray Walker; Vincent Neil Emerson

Sun Kil Moon.summary: Mark Kozelek's post-Red House Painters project extending that band's extended, confessional storytelling songwriting into the 2000s.

Sunday Mourners.summary: Los Angeles band blending frantic C86-style jangle-pop with post-punk urgency across a debut full of tightly wound guitar interplay.

Sunny Day Real Estate.summary: Seattle band whose Diary is considered the foundational second-wave emo album, launching a lineage that later fed twangy indie crossovers via American Football.

Sunny War.summary: Los Angeles (via Venice Beach busking) songwriter blending folk-punk fingerpicking with gospel, blues and roots textures on records featuring high-profile guests.

Superchunk.summary: Chapel Hill band co-founded by Mac McCaughan and Laura Ballance (also founders of Merge Records), whose hardcore-pop energy matured into melodic, occasionally orchestrated indie rock.

Superviolet.summary: Columbus, Ohio power-pop project in the Teenage Fanclub/Superchunk lineage, part of the 2020s power-pop revival.

Swampwater.summary: Nashville West alumnus Gib Guilbeau's loose, cajun-tinged country-rock band that began as Linda Ronstadt's backing group.

Swearin'.summary: Philadelphia band led by Allison Crutchfield and Kyle Gilbride playing scrappy, fuzzed-out guitar-pop out of the same DIY scene as Waxahatchee.

Sweethearts of the Rodeo.summary: Sister duo whose tight sibling-harmony country-rock, with Vince Gill guesting, put a rare female duo at the center of the mid-1980s neotraditional boom.

Swirlies.summary: Boston band whose shoestring, noise-collaged debut became the defining American shoegaze record and a direct forerunner of noisier countrygaze textures.

Sylvie.summary: Ben Schwab's Los Angeles trio project whose mostly-covers debut EP connects the LA psych scene to softer country-folk through a guest vocalist.

Symbol Soup.summary: London songwriter whose charming, conversational folk-rock moves at an ambling pace squarely in the wordy funny-sad Prine/Berman tradition.

T Bone Burnett.summary: Los Angeles songwriter (ex-Alpha Band, Bob Dylan's Rolling Thunder Revue) whose wry, unglamorous roots-rock records built his reputation as a roots theorist and future producer.

TOLEDO.summary: Brooklyn duo (Dan Alvarez de Toledo and Jordan Dunn-Pilz) built on finish-each-other's-sentences vocal harmony and family-history songwriting.

Tall Dwarfs.summary: Chris Knox and Alec Bathgate's Auckland duo whose home four-track, drum-machine pop directly prefigured American lo-fi acts like Guided by Voices and Sebadoh.
Tall Dwarfs.related: Toy Love; Guided by Voices; Sebadoh

Tammy Wynette.summary: Nashville singer whose Billy Sherrill-produced countrypolitan records defined the string-laden Epic sound of the late 1960s and became genre landmarks.

Tapir!.summary: UK sextet whose biblical, orchestrated art-folk concept album continues the chamber-folk tradition popularized by Sufjan Stevens into the current UK indie scene.

Tara Jane O'Neil.summary: Former Rodan bassist turned solo songwriter making knotty, patient records that veer between mesmerizing folk, psych drone and glitchy ambient textures.

Tarnation.summary: Paula Frazer's San Francisco project pairing a cinematic torch-singer voice with slow, pedal-steel country balladry, an odd but fitting fit on 4AD.

Tav Falco's Panther Burns.summary: Memphis outfit playing deliberately primitive, art-damaged rockabilly and blues rooted in the city's Sun Records-era tradition.

Te Huhu.summary: Auckland quartet mixing desert twang, brooding psych atmospherics and country phrasing into immersive, dynamically wide-ranging arrangements.

Teddy and the Rough Riders.summary: Nashville four-piece playing Dead-inspired psychedelic twang alongside rowdy garage energy, recorded live-in-the-room at Sam Phillips Recording.

Teenage Fanclub.summary: Glasgow band whose fuzzy 1990 debut evolved into the clearest 1990s heir to the Big Star/Byrds jangle-pop sound across a decade-plus Creation/Columbia run.

Teethe.summary: Texas slowcore band whose self-produced debut and richer, pedal-steel-laced follow-up refine dark, hushed indie rock.

Television.summary: New York band whose Marquee Moon traded punk's power chords for long, interlocking clean-guitar lines that directly influenced R.E.M. and Sonic Youth.

Tenci.summary: Chicago songwriter Jess Shoman's project pairing raw, cracked-voiced folk with a bandmate's saxophone and guitar in a whimsical, homespun style.

Terry.summary: Melbourne supergroup (members of Total Control, UV Race and Blank Realm) making wiry, deadpan guitar-pop that evolved into terse, hooky art-punk across four albums.
Terry.related: Total Control; UV Race; Blank Realm

Terry Allen.summary: Lubbock visual artist and songwriter whose conceptual debut and sprawling hometown song cycle turned satirical, gothic storytelling into a cult classic of the Texas songwriter scene.

Tex & the Horseheads.summary: LA band fronted by Texacala Jones fusing classic country-and-western phrasing with deathrock's darker, theatrical punk edge.

Th' Legendary Shack Shakers.summary: Kentucky band fronted by J.D. Wilkes mixing rockabilly, blues and punk into a manic, Southern-gothic revival-tent sound on Bloodshot Records.

The 3Ds.summary: Second-generation Dunedin band whose distorted, dual-vocalist guitar noise pushed the scene's jangle template toward American college-rock volume.

The Able Tasmans.summary: Auckland band built around Graeme Humphreys's tumbling piano rather than guitar, an odd, whimsical counterpoint to Flying Nun's guitar-heavy Dunedin sound.

The Allman Betts Band.summary: Band formed by the sons of three founding Allman Brothers Band members, recreating their fathers' twin-lead-guitar, jam-friendly sound almost note for note.

The Allman Brothers Band.summary: Macon, Georgia band whose twin-guitar, twin-drummer blues-and-jazz jams set the template for the whole Capricorn Southern-rock roster across a run of studio and live landmarks.

The Anomoanon.summary: Louisville project led by Will Oldham's brother, setting Robert Louis Stevenson's public-domain poems to spare country-folk on Oldham's own record label.

The Apples in Stereo.summary: Robert Schneider's Denver band whose lo-fi, tape-saturated Beach Boys/British Invasion pop founded the whole Elephant 6 Recording Company aesthetic.
The Apples in Stereo.related: Neutral Milk Hotel; The Olivia Tremor Control

The Band.summary: Dylan's former backing group whose warm, unhurried blend of country, gospel, R&B and rock reoriented a generation toward roots music.

The Bangles.summary: Los Angeles band whose tight, twelve-string power-pop debut preceded their mainstream pop years, made in the same early-'80s club scene as Paisley Underground peers.

The Bats.summary: Christchurch band formed by a former Clean drummer, playing the gentlest, most purely melodic jangle-pop to come out of the Flying Nun catalog.

The Beat Farmers.summary: San Diego band splitting vocal duties between a booming novelty baritone and straighter roots-rock songwriting, produced by Los Lobos's Steve Berlin.

The Belair Lip Bombs.summary: Melbourne band whose frenetic, interlocking power pop was produced by a member of Rolling Blackouts Coastal Fever.

The Beths.summary: Auckland band led by Elizabeth Stokes writing tight, guitar-heavy autobiographical power-pop that its own liner notes call a collision of pop and skuzz.

The Bird Calls.summary: Songwriting project drawing explicit comparison to David Berman, John Darnielle and Destroyer's Dan Bejar for its clever, plainspoken, folksy-yet-wry songs.
The Bird Calls.related: David Berman; Silver Jews; John Darnielle; Mountain Goats; Destroyer

The Black Swans.summary: Columbus, Ohio band led by Jerry DeCicca building a spare, haunted folk-rock sound that shares Songs: Ohia's Midwestern gothic atmosphere.

The Blasters.summary: Downey, California band (Dave and Phil Alvin) whose rockabilly-punk fusion became a cowpunk cornerstone and launchpad for the Knitters and X collaborations.

The Bongos.summary: Hoboken band whose ringing jangle pop founded the tiny club scene that later produced Yo La Tengo.

The Bottle Rockets.summary: Festus, Missouri band fronted by Brian Henneman (an Uncle Tupelo guest) whose loud Telecaster riffing and blunt working-class storytelling became a benchmark of insurgent country.

The Bug Club.summary: Welsh trio whose scrappy, deadpan-sung garage pop evolved from DIY ramshackle energy into a Sub Pop-signed, Modern Lovers/Nuggets-style sound.

The Byrds.summary: Los Angeles folk-rock pioneers whose chiming twelve-string harmonies evolved, once Gram Parsons joined, into the country-rock landmark that founded the whole genre.
The Byrds.related: Gram Parsons; The Flying Burrito Brothers; Clarence White

The Cannanes.summary: Sydney band whose scrappy, conversational lo-fi indie pop shared Flying Nun's homemade DIY spirit with a drier Australian sense of humor.

The Carter Family.summary: Foundational recorded country and folk act whose Appalachian hymns and ballads became the bedrock repertoire covered by generations of folk and country artists.

The Chills.summary: Dunedin band led by Martin Phillipps whose ringing, minor-key guitar pop spread the Flying Nun sound abroad before reaching commercial and orchestrated peaks.

The Clash.summary: UK punk band whose genre-sprawling double album fed directly into American cowpunk's own genre-crossing instincts.

The Clean.summary: Dunedin band (the Kilgour brothers and Robert Scott) whose cheap, motorik jangle-pop founded the whole Flying Nun sound and directly influenced Pavement and 1990s American lo-fi.
The Clean.related: The Chills; The Bats; Pavement; Yo La Tengo

The Clearwater Swimmers.summary: Maine-born, Queens-based band whose self-titled debut flips between hushed intimacy and full electric-guitar surges in the Neil Young/Jason Molina lineage.

The Connells.summary: Raleigh band whose ringing, R.E.M.-adjacent jangle extended the same Southern college-rock wave as its North Carolina peers.

The Convenience.summary: New Orleans slacker-pop trio delivering loose, deadpan-sung jangling guitar tracks in the same Crescent City DIY scene as a fellow local band.

The Dead C.summary: Dunedin band that pushed the scene's four-track amateurism to noise extremes, becoming a reference point for the American noise-rock underground.

The Dead Tongues.summary: Ryan Gustafson's Asheville project mixing fingerpicked guitar and banjo with warm full-band arrangements, tied closely to the region's cosmic-country web.
The Dead Tongues.related: Hiss Golden Messenger; Skyway Man; Mountain Man

The Decemberists.summary: Colin Meloy's Portland band whose orchestrated, literary chamber-folk theater built toward full prog-folk suites.

The Del-Lords.summary: New York band led by Dictators guitarist Scott Kempner, blending garage-rock crunch with country songwriting parallel to the LA cowpunk scene.

The Delines.summary: Willy Vlautin's post-Richmond Fontaine project centering singer Amy Boone's smoky voice on soul-tinged country storytelling about working-class characters.

The Desert Rose Band.summary: Chris Hillman's (Byrds, Flying Burrito Brothers) band with Herb Pedersen and John Jorgenson, turning '60s country-rock harmony into radio-ready neotraditional honky-tonk.
The Desert Rose Band.related: The Byrds; The Flying Burrito Brothers

The Deslondes.summary: New Orleans band mixing classic honky-tonk and 1950s rock and roll with a loose, communal multi-songwriter approach shared among several members.
The Deslondes.related: Hurray for the Riff Raff; Esther Rose

The Dexateens.summary: Tuscaloosa, Alabama band's garage-rock-scaled take on Southern storytelling rock, grungier than the more polished Muscle Shoals wing of the scene.
The Dexateens.related: Drive-By Truckers; Lee Bains III & the Glory Fires

The Dillards.summary: Ozarks bluegrass band, famous as the Byrds' backers, that plugged in and added strings and drums, arriving at country rock from the bluegrass side.

The Drams.summary: Band formed by Slobberbone frontman Brent Best and drummer Tony Harper with two members of a fellow Denton band after Slobberbone's initial breakup.

The Dream Syndicate.summary: Steve Wynn's LA band whose Velvet Underground/Neil Young-indebted feedback jams became the sound most identified with the Paisley Underground.
The Dream Syndicate.related: Green on Red; The Long Ryders; Rain Parade

The Embarrassment.summary: Wichita, Kansas band whose angular, new-wave-inflected guitar pop and deadpan small-town lyrics gave them an outsider, formative influence on later Midwest underground scenes.

The Everly Brothers.summary: Don and Phil Everly's brother-harmony duo whose old-ballad and country-rock records became a direct bridge to the Byrds and to Gram Parsons and Emmylou Harris's vocal blend.
The Everly Brothers.related: The Byrds; Gram Parsons; Emmylou Harris

The Feelies.summary: Haledon, New Jersey band whose nervy, interlocking-guitar debut (and a warmer, Peter Buck-produced follow-up) became a foundational influence on R.E.M. and jangle-pop.

The Felice Brothers.summary: Catskills band whose ramshackle, front-porch fiddle-and-accordion Americana made them heirs to The Band's rustic, communal storytelling.

The Flatlanders.summary: Jimmie Dale Gilmore, Joe Ely and Butch Hancock's Lubbock trio whose barely-released 1972 sessions became a legendary, spacey West Texas folk document once finally released in 1990.

The Flesh Eaters.summary: Chris D.'s one-off LA punk supergroup pulling members from X, the Blasters and Los Lobos for swampy, horn-streaked roots music under apocalyptic film-noir lyrics.
